title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
Much of R2D follows from two familiar words:
macrostate and microstate.
Statistical mechanics uses both constantly.
R2D asks a more primitive question:
The answer is the count boundary.
A microstate is not an intrinsically microscopic object.
A macrostate is not an intrinsically large object.
Both terms describe the relationship between a state and the boundary from which that state is counted.
Boundaries Define Scientific Objects →

title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
The Conventional Picture
A familiar description of statistical mechanics is:
\[
\text{microscopic reality}
\rightarrow
\text{coarse-grained macroscopic description}.
\]
On this picture, the microstate is often treated as the fully detailed underlying reality.
The macrostate is then a less detailed description obtained by ignoring some microscopic information.
This is often computationally useful.
But it leaves a foundational question unanswered:

What makes the underlying state a microstate in the first place?

R2D does not define “microstate” by physical size.
It defines it relative to a count boundary.

title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
The R2D Definition
Let the boundary of interest be
\[
B_n.
\]
Immediately subordinate to \(B_n\) is a collection of peer boundaries
\[
\{B_{n-1,\alpha}\}_{\alpha \in I_{n-1}}.
\]
Each subordinate peer boundary has its own possible realization domain.
Let
\[
\mathfrak{X}_{n-1,\alpha}
\]
denote the possible realization domain of peer \(\alpha\).
A complete joint peer realization has the form
\[
\mathbf{x}_{n-1}
=
\{x_{n-1,\alpha}\}_{\alpha \in I_{n-1}},
\]
where
\[
x_{n-1,\alpha}
\in
\mathfrak{X}_{n-1,\alpha}.
\]
If every combination of peer realizations were allowed, the complete product domain would be
\[
\prod_{\alpha \in I_{n-1}}
\mathfrak{X}_{n-1,\alpha}.
\]
But an enclosing boundary need not admit every formally imaginable combination.
Boundary \(B_n\) defines which joint realizations are compatible.
The compatible subset is the formal microstate domain:
\[
\mathfrak{M}_n
\subseteq
\prod_{\alpha \in I_{n-1}}
\mathfrak{X}_{n-1,\alpha}.
\]
A formal microstate at \(B_n\) is one compatible joint peer realization:
\[
\mu_n
=
\{x_{n-1,\alpha}\}_{\alpha \in I_{n-1}}
\in
\mathfrak{M}_n.
\]
This is the first formal definition.

A microstate at \(B_n\) is one compatible joint realization of the immediately subordinate peer boundaries.

It is not defined by being physically small.
It is defined by its relation to \(B_n\).

title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
The Macrostate Is a Classification
The enclosing boundary does not ordinarily distinguish every peer-resolved joint realization individually.
Instead, it classifies compatible formal microstates into states that are readable at \(B_n\).
Let
\[
\mathcal{M}_n
\]
be the readable macrostate set.
Define the classification map
\[
\pi_n:
\mathfrak{M}_n
\rightarrow
\mathcal{M}_n.
\]
If
\[
\pi_n(\mu_n)=i,
\]
then formal microstate \(\mu_n\) is read at boundary \(B_n\) as macrostate \(i\).
This gives the second definition:

A macrostate at \(B_n\) is a distinguishable classification of compatible formal microstates that is readable at \(B_n\).

The macrostate is therefore not primitively assembled by adding subordinate states together.
It is a boundary-defined classification.

title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
A Simple Example: Ten Coins
Suppose ten coins form one ensemble.
At the single-coin boundary, the readable states are
\[
H
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
T.
\]
Now change to the ten-coin boundary.
One formal microstate might be
\[
HHTHTHTTHH.
\]
Another might be
\[
THHHTHTHTH.
\]
These are distinct peer-resolved joint realizations.
But the ten-coin boundary may classify both simply by the number of heads.
If each realization contains six heads, then
\[
\pi_n(\mu_n)=6H.
\]
The ensemble macrostate is therefore
\[
N_H=6.
\]
Many different formal microstates belong to the same readable macrostate.
This is exactly what multiplicity counts.
The Coins Example →

title: Macrostate and Microstate
section: Multiplicity Is the Size of the Macrostate Class
text:
Multiplicity Is the Size of the Macrostate Class
For a macrostate \(i\), the complete set of formal microstates classified as \(i\) is the preimage
\[
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
=
\{
\mu_n \in \mathfrak{M}_n :
\pi_n(\mu_n)=i
\}.
\]
The notation
\[
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\]
means:

all formal microstates that the classification map \(\pi_n\) sends to macrostate \(i\).

Its cardinality is the multiplicity:
\[
\boxed{
W_{n,i}
=
\left|
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\right|
}
\]
The vertical bars mean the number of members in the set.
So:
\[
W_{n,i}
\]
is the number of compatible joint peer realizations that boundary \(B_n\) classifies as macrostate \(i\).
Its logarithmic coordinate is
\[
S_{n,i}
=
\ln W_{n,i}.
\]
At this stage, \(S\) is not yet thermodynamic entropy.
It is the logarithmic coordinate of multiplicity.
Multiplicity →

title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
Three Different Mathematical Objects
It is important not to collapse microstate, macrostate, and multiplicity into one idea.
They are three different things:
\[
\boxed{
\mu_n
=
\text{one compatible joint peer realization}
}
\]
\[
\boxed{
i
=
\text{the readable classification of that realization at } B_n
}
\]
\[
\boxed{
W_{n,i}
=
\text{the number of compatible realizations classified as } i
}
\]
A microstate is a realization.
A macrostate is a classification.
Multiplicity is a count of compatible realizations belonging to that classification.

title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
The Boundary Owns the Classification
The classification map
\[
\pi_n
\]
belongs to boundary \(B_n\).
Change the boundary and the classification changes.
This means a formal microstate at \(B_n\) does not simply remain the same microstate at \(B_{n+1}\).
The enclosing boundary defines:

a different peer realization domain;
a different compatibility relation;
a different formal microstate space;
and a different classification map.

Therefore:
\[
\boxed{
B_n \rightarrow B_{n+1}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{new state domain}
}
\]
Changing the boundary changes what counts as a state.
This is why R2D treats scientific objecthood as boundary dependent.
Scientific Objecthood →

title: Macrostate and Microstate
section: A Macrostate at One Boundary Can Have Microstate Meaning at Another
text:
A Macrostate at One Boundary Can Have Microstate Meaning at Another
This is one of the most important consequences.
Suppose a transition
\[
u \rightarrow v
\]
is directly readable at subordinate boundary
\[
B_{n-1,\alpha}.
\]
At that boundary, \(u\) and \(v\) are macrostates.
The transition is a readable macrostate transition.
Now consider the same physical occurrence from enclosing boundary \(B_n\).
The individual subordinate peer transition is no longer the state being classified.
It participates in a joint realization of the peer ensemble.
Relative to \(B_n\), the same subordinate change therefore has microstate meaning.
Schematically:
\[
\boxed{
\text{macrostate transition at } B_{n-1}
=
\text{microstate transition relative to } B_n
}
\]
The physical occurrence has not necessarily changed.
Its count meaning has.

title: Macrostate and Microstate
section: Microstate Does Not Mean Hidden Little Object
text:
Microstate Does Not Mean Hidden Little Object
This distinction is easy to miss.
R2D does not say that the microstate is a tiny physical object hiding beneath the macrostate.
A formal microstate is mathematically defined relative to the enclosing classification.
Its complete peer-resolved identity may be formally specified without being individually readable from the enclosing boundary.
Thus:

Defined does not imply readable.

Boundary \(B_n\) can classify a joint realization without resolving which subordinate peer transition produced it.
This is the primitive source of a distinction that later becomes important in both quantum and many-body descriptions.

title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
The Primitive Observer Effect
Suppose a microstate transition relative to \(B_n\) is not directly readable.
How can the observer see it?
The observer must change to the subordinate boundary where that distinction is readable as a macrostate transition.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\text{resolution}
\rightarrow
\text{change of count boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{change of state classification}
}
\]
This gives R2D a primitive observer effect before particles, measuring devices, wavefunctions, or quantum mechanics have been introduced.
Observation does not need to begin by physically perturbing an independently fixed microscopic state.
Increasing resolution changes the boundary from which the state is classified.
And therefore changes what the state is relative to the count.

title: Macrostate and Microstate
section: Why Better Resolution Does Not Recover One Fixed Ontology
text:
Why Better Resolution Does Not Recover One Fixed Ontology
Consider the ten-coin ensemble again.
At the ensemble boundary, the question might be:

Why does the ten-coin system occupy \(N_H=6\) rather than \(N_H=5\)?

If we increase resolution and follow one particular coin, the question becomes:

Why did this coin change from \(H\) to \(T\)?

The second question does not reveal the hidden detailed answer to the first.
It is a different question at a different boundary.
The object has changed.
The state domain has changed.
The causal relation being investigated has changed.
This is why R2D rejects the assumption that causal explanation can always be made more fundamental merely by increasing resolution.

title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
This Is Not Ordinary Coarse-Graining
The conventional coarse-graining picture can be written schematically as
\[
\text{same underlying microscopic state}
\rightarrow
\text{less detailed macroscopic description}.
\]
R2D instead proposes
\[
\boxed{
\text{boundary change}
\rightarrow
\text{state-domain replacement}
}
\]
The subordinate realization may remain physically consequential.
But it does not retain the same classification, path identity, or source identity at the enclosing boundary.
A macrostate is therefore not merely a blurry microstate.
And a microstate is not merely a sharper macrostate.
They belong to different boundary-relative count relations.
Why R²D Is Not Coarse-Graining →

title: Macrostate and Microstate
text:
Why This Matters for Causality
Suppose one tries to place directional causality entirely inside the microstate transitions.
At boundary \(B_n\), however, those transitions are not individually readable as microstate transitions.
To define their direction directly, one must move to \(B_{n-1}\), where the same transition has macrostate meaning.
But at that boundary, its directional relation is itself defined relative to its enclosing compatibility.
So moving the proposed cause “down into the microstates” does not escape the recursive architecture.
It changes the count boundary.
Schematically:
\[
\text{microstate at } B_n
\longrightarrow
\text{macrostate at } B_{n-1}
\longrightarrow
\text{enclosing relation at } B_n.
\]
This motivates the later R2D distinction between:
local realization
and
enclosing directional organization.

=
-
\lambda_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
}
\]
Its magnitude,
\[
\left|
\lambda_{n,i\rightarrow k}
\right|,
\]
gives the size of the distinction.
No primitive spatial, mechanical, energetic, or temporal interpretation has yet been assigned.

title: Constraint and Retention
section: Constraint Comes From the Enclosing Relation
text:
Constraint Comes From the Enclosing Relation
The local transition is defined at \(B_n\).
The relevant constraint is defined by the enclosing count relation at
\[
B_{n+1}.
\]
Write the total enclosing constraint as
\[
C_{n+1} \geq 0.
\]
This placement is important.
Just as possibility is defined through compatibility with the enclosing boundary, constraint is also an enclosing relation.
Thus the local transition does not contain within itself the complete relation that organizes its realization.
Schematically,
\[
\boxed{
B_{n+1}
\longrightarrow
\text{constraint on realization at } B_n.
}
\]

title: Constraint and Retention
section: Retention Requires Both Constraint and Distinguishability
text:
Retention Requires Both Constraint and Distinguishability
For the readable transition
\[
i \rightarrow k,
\]
local retention is
\[
\boxed{
\Delta R_{n,i\rightarrow k}
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\lambda_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
}
\]
This equation contains two logically distinct quantities.

Constraint
\[
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\]
specifies the productive/output component of the enclosing constraint.


Distinguishability
\[
\lambda_{n,i\rightarrow k}
\]
specifies the readable local interval against which that constraint acts.
Both are required.
If
\[
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}=0,
\]
then
\[
\Delta R=0
\]
even when a local distinction exists.
Likewise, if
\[
\lambda_{n,i\rightarrow k}=0,
\]
then
\[
\Delta R=0
\]
even when enclosing constraint is present.
Therefore:

Constraint without distinguishability produces no local retention.

and

Distinguishability without productive constraint produces no local retention.

title: Constraint and Retention
section: Distinguishability Is Not Created by Constraint
text:
Distinguishability Is Not Created by Constraint
The existence of a readable distinction does not require productive constraint.
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}=0
\quad\not\Rightarrow\quad
\lambda_n=0.
}
\]
A transition can remain distinguishable even when none of its directional possibility is retained as productive output.
This separation becomes important later when the same physical system can possess a readable distinction under zero productive load.
Constraint determines retention of a distinction.
It does not primitively define whether the distinction exists.

title: Constraint and Retention
Constraint and Retention
text:
Retention Is Oriented
Because
\[
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}} > 0
\]
and the distinguishable interval is oriented, retention inherits the orientation of the transition.
Thus,
\[
\Delta R_{n,k\rightarrow i}
=
-
\Delta R_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
\]
The sign therefore comes from
\[
\lambda.
\]
The constraint magnitude need not itself reverse sign.
This lets R2D distinguish:

the magnitude of constraint;
the magnitude of the distinction;
and the orientation of the transition.

That separation later becomes useful when physical quantities such as mechanical direction, charge, or spatial orientation are introduced.

title: Constraint and Retention
section: Possibility and Retention Are Different Relations
text:
Possibility and Retention Are Different Relations
For a local transition
\[
i \rightarrow k,
\]
directional possibility is
\[
\Delta P_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
\]
Retention is
\[
\Delta R_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
\]
They should not be identified.
Possibility asks:

How differently do the two local alternatives participate in compatible enclosing realizations?

Retention asks:

How much of that directional possibility is retained against the readable local distinction?

Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\Delta P
\neq
\Delta R.
}
\]
Their difference defines the remaining local asymmetry:
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A
=
\Delta P
-
\Delta R.
}
\]
Asymmetry →

title: Constraint and Retention
text:
Three Regimes
The relation
\[
\Delta A
=
\Delta P-\Delta R
\]
immediately gives three important cases.

Incomplete retention
If
\[
\Delta R < \Delta P,
\]
then
\[
\Delta A>0.
\]
Some directional possibility remains available for local realization.


Complete retention
If
\[
\boxed{
\Delta R=\Delta P,
}
\]
then
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A=0.
}
\]
This is the R2D stall condition.
The directional possibility has not disappeared.
It has been completely retained.


Retention greater than directional possibility
If
\[
\Delta R>\Delta P,
\]
then
\[
\Delta A<0.
\]
The local directional asymmetry reverses.
These regimes are developed more fully in the next section.
Asymmetry →

title: Constraint and Retention
text:
Zero Retention Is Not Stall
Another important distinction follows immediately.
If
\[
\Delta R=0,
\]
then
\[
\Delta A=\Delta P.
\]
All of the directional possibility remains locally available.
That is very different from stall.
At stall,
\[
\Delta R=\Delta P
\]
and therefore
\[
\Delta A=0.
\]
So two apparently quiet or zero-output limits can have opposite meanings.
One can correspond to no productive retention.
The other corresponds to complete retention.
This distinction later becomes directly readable in muscle mechanics.

title: Constraint and Retention
section: Why Mechanical Load Is a Useful Example
text:
Why Mechanical Load Is a Useful Example
Muscle provides an especially clear physical calibration.
A myosin transition has a mechanically distinguishable interval.
In a suitable physical mapping,
\[
\lambda_n
\longrightarrow
d,
\]
where \(d\) is a myosin-scale displacement.
The productive constraint acquires a force coordinate,
\[
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\longrightarrow
F.
\]
Then local retention acquires the energetic read
\[
\Delta R
\longrightarrow
Fd.
\]
This is a physical calibration of the primitive relation
\[
\Delta R
=
C^{\mathrm{out}}\lambda.
\]
It does not define \(C\) primitively as force or \(\lambda\) primitively as distance.
The count relation comes first.
The mechanical interpretation comes later.

title: Constraint and Retention
section: Changing Constraint Need Not Change Multiplicity
text:
Changing Constraint Need Not Change Multiplicity
This provides a clean separation among several quantities.
Suppose the native multiplicity landscape remains fixed:
\[
\mathcal{W}_n
=
\{W_{n,i}\}.
\]
Suppose the enclosing possibility relation also remains fixed.
Changing the productive constraint can still change
\[
\Delta R.
\]
Therefore it can change
\[
\Delta A.
\]
And because asymmetry biases occupancy, the realized state distribution can change.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\text{changing constraint}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{changing native multiplicity}.
}
\]
A system can move through different realized states of the same multiplicity landscape because its enclosing constraint has changed.
This distinction is particularly useful in systems such as muscle, where mechanical load can be varied experimentally while the molecular state architecture remains present.

title: Constraint and Retention
section: Total Constraint and Productive Constraint Are Not the Same
text:
Total Constraint and Productive Constraint Are Not the Same
The local retention equation uses only the productive/output component
\[
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}.
\]
But the total enclosing constraint can contain more than one readable component.
R2D writes
\[
\boxed{
C_{n+1}
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
+
C_{n+1}^{\Phi}.
}
\]
Here
\[
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\]
is associated with realization that remains readable as distinguishable output.
The term
\[
C_{n+1}^{\Phi}
\]
is the background-associated constraint component.
The two act on the same enclosing transition.
They are not two separate physical transitions.
They are not two independent occurrence pathways.
They are two boundary-specific readings associated with one enclosing realization.

title: Constraint and Retention
section: Local Retention Uses the Productive Component
text:
Local Retention Uses the Productive Component
At the local boundary,
\[
\boxed{
\Delta R_n
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\lambda_n.
}
\]
Only the productive/output component enters local retention.
The background-associated component is not added to \(\Delta R_n\).
This preserves an important distinction:

local retention is not the same quantity as total enclosing constraint.

At the enclosing boundary, however, the full constraint
\[
C_{n+1}
\]
enters the recurrence-weighted R2D law.
That law therefore connects two different boundary-specific reads of the same recursively organized relation.
The R²D Law →

title: Constraint and Retention
text:
Productive and Background-Associated Constraint
The decomposition can be summarized as
\[
\boxed{
C_{n+1}
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
+
C_{n+1}^{\Phi}.
}
\]
The productive constrained distinguishability is
\[
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}\lambda_{n+1}.
\]
The background-associated constrained distinguishability is
\[
C_{n+1}^{\Phi}\lambda_{n+1}.
\]
These are distinct reads of the same enclosing occurrence.
The existence of the background-associated component does not mean that background itself is a third directed local coordinate.
The relationship between local nonreciprocal occurrence realization and enclosing background is introduced separately by the R2D Second Law.
The R²D Second Law →

title: Constraint and Retention
text:
Constraint Does Not “Push” the Component
The equation
\[
\Delta R
=
C^{\mathrm{out}}\lambda
\]
can invite a mechanical picture in which constraint physically pushes against a component.
That interpretation is too specific for Part I.
R2D has not yet defined a particle, force, trajectory, or spatial displacement.
The more primitive statement is:

An enclosing constraint acts across a boundary-readable distinction and thereby retains part of the directional possibility associated with that distinction.

A later physical theory can decide how that relation is measured.

title: Constraint and Retention
Constraint and Retention
Constraint and Retention
Constraint and Retention
text:
The Key Distinction
The simplest summary is:

\(\lambda\) defines the readable difference.


\(C^{\mathrm{out}}\) defines the productive constraint acting across that difference.


\(\Delta R=C^{\mathrm{out}}\lambda\) is the possibility retained against the distinguishable change.

Possibility and retention can now be compared directly.
Their difference is local asymmetry.

title: Closure
text:
A state can change and return to where it began.
That is a return.
But R2D gives closure a more specific meaning.
A local return becomes a closure when that completed path is compatible with an occurrence at the enclosing boundary.
Thus:
This distinction matters because the local state can close even when the enclosing relations organizing its forward and return paths do not.
That is the basis of asymmetric closure.

title: Closure
text:
A Macrostate Return
At boundary \(B_n\), consider a finite readable path
\[
\mathcal{R}_n:
i_0
\rightarrow
i_1
\rightarrow
\cdots
\rightarrow
i_m.
\]
If
\[
i_m=i_0,
\]
the path has returned to its initial macrostate.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal{R}_n:
i_0
\rightarrow
i_1
\rightarrow
\cdots
\rightarrow
i_0
}
\]
is a macrostate return.
A return is defined entirely by the local state path.
No statement about the enclosing relation has yet been made.

title: Closure
text:
Return Is Not Yet Closure
Now consider the enclosing boundary
\[
B_{n+1}.
\]
If the completed local return is compatible with at least one enclosing occurrence at \(B_{n+1}\), R2D calls it a closure.
For peer boundary \(\alpha\), write
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}.
}
\]
So:
\[
\boxed{
\text{return}
+
\text{compatibility with an enclosing occurrence}
=
\text{closure}.
}
\]
The local path is readable at \(B_n\).
Its enclosing significance belongs to \(B_{n+1}\).
This is what makes closure a recursive rather than merely cyclic concept.
Recursive Carry →

title: Closure
text:
The Minimal Closure
The simplest closure has two opposed legs:
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal{C}_{n,\alpha}:
i
\rightarrow
k
\rightarrow
i.
}
\]
The first leg is
\[
i\rightarrow k,
\]
and the return leg is
\[
k\rightarrow i.
\]
The local state closes because the final macrostate equals the initial macrostate.
But this does not require the two legs to occur under identical enclosing conditions.
That is the key point.

title: Closure
section: Local Reversal Does Not Require Enclosing Reversal
text:
Local Reversal Does Not Require Enclosing Reversal
Suppose the forward leg
\[
i\rightarrow k
\]
is realized under enclosing condition \(H\).
Suppose the return leg
\[
k\rightarrow i
\]
is realized under enclosing condition \(L\).
The local transition has reversed.
But the enclosing compatibility relation need not have reversed.
The extension multiplicities can therefore differ between the two branches:
\[
K_{n+1|n,i}^{H},
\qquad
K_{n+1|n,k}^{H},
\]
and
\[
K_{n+1|n,i}^{L},
\qquad
K_{n+1|n,k}^{L}.
\]
Likewise, the enclosing productive constraints need not be identical on the two legs.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\text{local path reversal}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{reversal of the enclosing relation}.
}
\]
This is the primitive structure of asymmetric closure.

title: Closure
Closure
Closure
section: Constraint Can Also Differ Around the Closure
text:
Constraint Can Also Differ Around the Closure
The two branches can also experience different productive constraints.
For the forward leg,
\[
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,H}
=
C_{n+1,H}^{\mathrm{out}}
\lambda_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow k}.
\]
For the return leg,
\[
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,L}
=
C_{n+1,L}^{\mathrm{out}}
\lambda_{n,\alpha,k\rightarrow i}.
\]
Because distinguishability is oriented,
\[
\lambda_{n,\alpha,k\rightarrow i}
=
-
\lambda_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow k}.
\]
But the enclosing constraints themselves need not be equal:
\[
C_{n+1,H}^{\mathrm{out}}
\neq
C_{n+1,L}^{\mathrm{out}}.
\]
Therefore the two retention terms need not cancel.
Constraint and Retention →

title: Closure
Closure
Closure
text:
The Most Important Closure Result
The local path
\[
i\rightarrow k\rightarrow i
\]
returns exactly.
But the enclosing relation need not.
That gives the central distinction:
\[
\boxed{
\text{local state closure}
\neq
\text{closure of the enclosing directional relation}.
}
\]
A locally closed cycle can therefore remain directionally organized.
This is what makes a turbine-like cycle possible in R2D.
The local machine returns.
The relation driving its opposed branches need not.

title: Closure
text:
Native Multiplicity Closes Exactly
The local multiplicity difference for the forward transition is
\[
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow k}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{W_{n,k}}{W_{n,i}}
\right).
\]
For the return,
\[
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,k\rightarrow i}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{W_{n,i}}{W_{n,k}}
\right).
\]
Adding them gives
\[
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow k}
+
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,k\rightarrow i}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0.
}
\]
This is exact.
The native multiplicity ratios are reciprocal because the state path has returned within the same native multiplicity landscape.

title: Closure
section: Multiplicity Closure Does Not Imply Possibility Closure
text:
Multiplicity Closure Does Not Imply Possibility Closure
The equation
\[
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0
\]
does not imply
\[
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0.
\]
These quantities belong to different relations.
Native multiplicity is defined within the local boundary.
Possibility is defined through compatibility with the enclosing boundary.
Thus a closure can satisfy simultaneously
\[
\boxed{
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}\neq0.
}
\]
This is one of the cleanest examples of why R2D keeps local and enclosing count relations separate.

title: Closure
section: Multiplicity Closure Does Not Imply Asymmetry Closure
text:
Multiplicity Closure Does Not Imply Asymmetry Closure
Likewise,
\[
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0
\]
does not imply
\[
\Delta A_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0.
\]
The local multiplicity can return exactly while the enclosing-defined possibility-retention relation remains asymmetric.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}=0
\qquad\text{while}\qquad
\Delta A_{\mathcal C}\neq0
}
\]
is perfectly consistent.
The first statement concerns possible local structure.
The second concerns enclosing directional organization.

title: Closure
section: A Turbine Makes the Distinction Intuitive
text:
A Turbine Makes the Distinction Intuitive
Imagine a turbine blade returning to the same position after one revolution.
Locally:
\[
\text{position}
\rightarrow
\text{different position}
\rightarrow
\text{original position}.
\]
The blade has completed a return.
But the pressure difference across the turbine need not have disappeared.
The local mechanical path closes.
The enclosing directional relation remains.
That is the intuitive form of asymmetric closure:

The local structure returns while the larger relation organizing the cycle need not.

R2D abstracts this architecture away from the particular mechanical example.

title: Closure
text:
Muscle Provides a Biological Example
Muscle also contains cyclic local realization.
Molecular switches can repeatedly move among states.
At steady shortening, the ensemble can maintain a statistically stable local cycle while ATP free-energy relations and mechanical load continue to organize the cycle.
The molecular states recur.
The enclosing chemical-mechanical relation does not have to disappear each time one molecular cycle closes.
Again:
\[
\boxed{
\text{local recurrence}
\neq
\text{loss of enclosing direction}.
}
\]
This is why closure is especially important for biological steady states.

title: Closure
text:
Occurrence Around a Closure
So far, closure has described the state path.
But the two opposed legs can also be counted as realized occurrences.
Let
\[
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
\]
be the number of completed realizations of the forward oriented leg \(H\),
and
\[
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
\]
the number of completed realizations of the opposed leg \(L\),
within a specified finite realization domain.
These are path occurrence counts.
They are not simply sums of state occurrence counts along the path.
Define
\[
\tau_{n,\alpha,H}
=
\ln\nu_{n,\alpha,H},
\]
and
\[
\tau_{n,\alpha,L}
=
\ln\nu_{n,\alpha,L}.
\]
This introduces another closure question:

Are the two opposed legs realized equally often?

title: Closure
text:
State-Occurrence Closure Is Exact
The state occurrence coordinate for macrostate \(i\) is
\[
\tau_{n,i}
=
\ln\nu_{n,i}.
\]
For a genuine closed state path, the signed transition differences telescope:
\[
\boxed{
\sum_{\chi\in\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}}
\Delta\tau_{n,\alpha,\chi}
=
0.
}
\]
This says that the state-defined occurrence coordinate returns with the closed state path.
It does not mean that the two complete opposed legs occur equally often.
That is a separate count relation.

title: Closure
Closure
text:
Nonreciprocal Occurrence Realization
If
\[
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
<
\nu_{n,\alpha,H},
\]
then
\[
\boxed{
0<
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
<1.
}
\]
The two opposed legs are realized with unequal directional efficiency.
Define the logarithmic opposed-leg difference
\[
\Delta\tau_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\ln\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
\]
Then nonreciprocity gives
\[
\Delta\tau_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}<0.
\]
This does not mean occurrence has been destroyed.
It means the opposed directions are realized with unequal count efficiency.

title: Closure
section: Closure Asymmetry and Occurrence Nonreciprocity Are Not the Same
text:
Closure Asymmetry and Occurrence Nonreciprocity Are Not the Same
This distinction is essential.
A closure can have
\[
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}\neq0
\]
while still satisfying
\[
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=1.
\]
Or it can have
\[
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}\neq0
\]
together with
\[
0<
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
<1.
\]
Therefore:
\[
\boxed{
\text{asymmetric enclosing organization}
\not\equiv
\text{nonreciprocal occurrence realization}.
}
\]
The first concerns possibility and retention.
The second concerns the realized occurrence counts of the opposed closure legs.
They must remain distinct.

title: Closure
Closure
text:
Four Different Closure Questions
A completed closure therefore contains several mathematically different questions.

Did the local state return?
For a closure,
\[
i\rightarrow k\rightarrow i.
\]
Yes.


Did native multiplicity close?
Yes:
\[
\boxed{
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}=0.
}
\]


Did enclosing asymmetry close?
Not necessarily:
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A_{\mathcal C}
\neq0
}
\]
is allowed.


Were the opposed legs realized reciprocally?
Not necessarily:
\[
\boxed{
0<\eta_{\mathcal C}<1
}
\]
is allowed.
These statements must not be collapsed into one notion of “closure” or “irreversibility.”

title: Closure
text:
Recurrence Is Yet Another Count
There is still one more question:

How many times does the completed closure recur?

That question is not answered by
\[
\Delta S_{\mathcal C},
\]
by
\[
\Delta A_{\mathcal C},
\]
or by
\[
\eta_{\mathcal C}.
\]
It requires a separate whole-closure recurrence count.
Thus R2D separates:
\[
\boxed{
\text{state return}
}
\]
from
\[
\boxed{
\text{directional asymmetry}
}
\]
from
\[
\boxed{
\text{opposed-leg occurrence reciprocity}
}
\]
from
\[
\boxed{
\text{number of closure recurrences}.
}
\]
Recurrence →

title: Closure
text:
Closure Makes Recursive Carry Possible
Once a local realization has completed its return, it can be treated as one completed relation at the local boundary.
When the count boundary changes, that completed local relation need not remain readable through its internal path.
Instead, it can acquire enclosing occurrence meaning.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
}
\]
Closure therefore supplies the completed local realization that recursive carry can reclassify.
The local path is readable below.
Its enclosing meaning is readable above.
Recursive Carry →

title: Closure
text:
Closure Is Not Upward Causation
This does not mean that the completed closure creates the enclosing occurrence.
Causally, R2D retains the opposite orientation:
\[
\boxed{
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}.
}
\]
The enclosing occurrence defines its compatible local realization.
The completed local closure is then reclassified when the count boundary changes.
Thus:

Closure completes the local realization.


It does not generate the enclosing organization from below.

The Causal Inversion →

title: Closure
section: What Closes and What Need Not Close

title: Closure
text:
The Key Distinction
Closure is therefore not simply “coming back to the beginning.”
It is a layered recursive structure.
The local macrostate returns.
Native multiplicity closes exactly.
But the enclosing relation organizing the opposed legs can remain asymmetric.
The realization of those legs can remain nonreciprocal.
And the completed closure can recur at its own count relative to the enclosing boundary.
That separation allows R2D to distinguish cycle, direction, irreversibility, and recurrence before assigning physical units to any of them.

title: Boundaries Define Scientific Objects
text:
R2D begins with the principle:

Counting requires distinguishability.

But distinguishability alone is not enough.
A scientific count also requires a boundary that determines what counts as a distinction.
R2D therefore makes the boundary primitive to the scientific object.

A boundary defines the count domain.

The boundary does not merely surround an already-defined object.
It participates in defining what the object is.


In ordinary language, a boundary often means a wall, membrane, surface, or spatial edge.
That is not the primitive R2D definition.
A boundary is the relation that determines:

which differences are distinguishable;
which subordinate realizations are mutually compatible;
which compatible realizations belong to the same readable state;
and which completed subordinate processes count as realizations of an enclosing occurrence.

A membrane can define a boundary.
So can an ensemble definition.
So can an experimental measurement.
So can the distinction between one molecular state and another.
The primitive requirement is not a physical surface.
It is a count domain.



Consider a single coin.
At one boundary, the readable states are
\[
H
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
T.
\]
The coin is the object.
Now consider ten coins together.
At the ensemble boundary, the readable states might instead be
\[
(10H,0T),\;
(9H,1T),\;
\dots,\;
(0H,10T).
\]
The ten-coin ensemble is now the object.
The individual heads and tails have not disappeared physically.
But they no longer possess the same state meaning at the ensemble boundary.
The boundary has changed.
Therefore the count domain has changed.
Therefore the scientific object has changed.
Work through the coins example →



This distinction becomes especially important in science.
Consider water.
At one boundary, the scientific object may be a water molecule.
Its readable states belong to the molecular state domain.
At another boundary, the scientific object may be a glass of water.
Its readable states belong to an enclosing thermodynamic or mechanical state domain.
The water is not a poorly resolved water molecule.
And the molecule is not highly resolved water.
They are different scientific objects because they are defined at different count boundaries.
R2D therefore rejects the assumption that increasing or decreasing resolution always reveals more or less detail about one ontologically fixed object.
Instead:
\[
\boxed{
\text{change boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{change count domain}
\rightarrow
\text{change scientific object}
}
\]



Statistical mechanics itself provides an important clue.
The same combinatorial mathematics can describe an ensemble of:

spins;
electrons;
molecules;
proteins;
molecular motors;
cells;
coins;
or other distinguishable systems.

Nothing in the combinatorics declares one of these objects to be the uniquely fundamental scale.
A protein can be the object.
A molecular state within that protein can be the object.
An ensemble of proteins can be the object.
A muscle fiber can be the object.
Which one is being counted depends on the boundary.

Science is boundary dependent. It does not privilege one object or one scale.




This leads directly to the most important definitions in R2D.
A state does not first exist independently of the boundary and then receive a label such as “microstate” or “macrostate.”
Those terms describe a relationship to a boundary.
At boundary \(B_n\):

a macrostate is a distinguishable state readable at \(B_n\);
a formal microstate is one compatible joint realization of the immediately subordinate peer boundaries.

The distinction is relational.
A state can therefore have macrostate meaning at one boundary and microstate meaning relative to another.
Macrostate and Microstate →



Suppose the boundary being considered is
\[
B_n.
\]
Let its immediately subordinate peer boundaries be
\[
B_{n-1,\alpha}.
\]
Each subordinate peer possesses its own state domain.
A realization of the enclosing boundary involves some joint realization of those peers.
Not every formally imaginable combination must be compatible.
The enclosing boundary \(B_n\) determines which joint peer realizations belong to its admissible count domain.
Schematically:
\[
\text{peer realizations}
\rightarrow
\text{compatibility at } B_n
\rightarrow
\text{state domain at } B_n.
\]
This is why the enclosing boundary is not simply a passive container.
It defines the relation under which subordinate realizations count together.



Once the boundary has defined which subordinate realizations are compatible, those realizations can be classified into readable states.
If many compatible subordinate realizations are classified as the same readable state, that state has multiplicity.
Thus the logical order is:
\[
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{compatible realizations}
\rightarrow
\text{classification}
\rightarrow
\text{multiplicity}
}
\]
Multiplicity therefore does not create the boundary.
The boundary defines the count domain in which multiplicity can be counted.
Understand Multiplicity →



This has an important consequence for observation.
Suppose a subordinate transition is not individually readable at \(B_n\).
One might imagine that better experimental resolution simply reveals that hidden transition while leaving the scientific description unchanged.
R2D says something more precise.
To read the subordinate transition directly, the observer must move to the subordinate boundary where that transition is distinguishable.
But once the boundary changes, the state classification changes too.
The transition that had microstate meaning relative to \(B_n\) now has macrostate meaning at \(B_{n-1}\).
Therefore:
\[
\boxed{
\text{increased resolution}
\rightarrow
\text{change of boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{change of state meaning}
}
\]
Observation has not merely revealed more detail about the same formal state.
It has changed the count domain from which the state is defined.



Return to the ten-coin example.
At the ten-coin boundary, one may ask:

Why does the ensemble occupy one macrostate rather than another?

To resolve an individual coin transition, the observer changes to the single-coin boundary.
The question is now:

Why does this coin realize heads rather than tails?

These are not the same causal question at different resolutions.
They belong to different count domains.
This matters because bottom-up causation is often inferred by resolving smaller and smaller mechanisms.
R2D warns that increasing resolution changes the boundary from which causality is being defined.
A subordinate mechanism can be necessary for the realization of an enclosing state without therefore being the source of the organization that distinguishes the enclosing state.
The Causal Inversion →



The difference from ordinary coarse-graining is fundamental.
A coarse-graining picture often suggests:
\[
\text{same underlying state}
\rightarrow
\text{less information}.
\]
R2D instead proposes:
\[
\text{new boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{new classification}
\rightarrow
\text{new state domain}.
\]
The subordinate realization can remain physically consequential.
But its internal path, source identity, and state classification need not remain readable as the same objects from the enclosing boundary.
Changing the boundary is therefore not merely forgetting information.
It changes the ontology of the count.
Why R²D Is Not Coarse-Graining →



Once statehood is boundary dependent, recursive replacement follows naturally.
A subordinate state is readable at its own boundary.
When an enclosing boundary becomes the count domain, the subordinate distinctions no longer remain the states being counted.
Their compatible realizations instead participate in defining the multiplicity and state structure of the enclosing object.
Thus:
\[
\text{subordinate state domain}
\rightarrow
\text{boundary change}
\rightarrow
\text{enclosing state domain}.
\]
The subordinate object has not been erased.
Its count meaning has changed.
R2D calls this operation recursive replacement.
Recursive Replacement →



The broader implication is straightforward.
A particle can be real.
A molecule can be real.
A protein can be real.
A cell can be real.
A muscle can be real.
A planet can be real.
A spacetime metric can be real.
R2D does not require any of them to be illusions.
It requires only that their scientific identity be indexed to the boundary that makes their states distinguishable.
A scientific object can therefore be:

completely real;
measurable;
predictive;
and causally useful

without being primitive at every scale.
This is why R2D is not merely a theory about particular objects.
It is a proposed theory of scientific objecthood.
Scientific Objecthood →



The primitive sequence can now be expanded:
\[
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{compatible realization}
\rightarrow
\text{state classification}
\rightarrow
\text{count}
}
\]
The scientific object appears only after the count domain has been defined.
This is the inversion at the foundation of R2D:

The boundary does not merely tell us where the object is.
The boundary helps define what the object is.

title: Boundaries Define Scientific Objects
text:
In ordinary language, a boundary often means a wall, membrane, surface, or spatial edge.
That is not the primitive R2D definition.
A boundary is the relation that determines:

which differences are distinguishable;
which subordinate realizations are mutually compatible;
which compatible realizations belong to the same readable state;
and which completed subordinate processes count as realizations of an enclosing occurrence.

A membrane can define a boundary.
So can an ensemble definition.
So can an experimental measurement.
So can the distinction between one molecular state and another.
The primitive requirement is not a physical surface.
It is a count domain.

title: Boundaries Define Scientific Objects
text:
Consider a single coin.
At one boundary, the readable states are
\[
H
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
T.
\]
The coin is the object.
Now consider ten coins together.
At the ensemble boundary, the readable states might instead be
\[
(10H,0T),\;
(9H,1T),\;
\dots,\;
(0H,10T).
\]
The ten-coin ensemble is now the object.
The individual heads and tails have not disappeared physically.
But they no longer possess the same state meaning at the ensemble boundary.
The boundary has changed.
Therefore the count domain has changed.
Therefore the scientific object has changed.
Work through the coins example →

title: Boundaries Define Scientific Objects
text:
This distinction becomes especially important in science.
Consider water.
At one boundary, the scientific object may be a water molecule.
Its readable states belong to the molecular state domain.
At another boundary, the scientific object may be a glass of water.
Its readable states belong to an enclosing thermodynamic or mechanical state domain.
The water is not a poorly resolved water molecule.
And the molecule is not highly resolved water.
They are different scientific objects because they are defined at different count boundaries.
R2D therefore rejects the assumption that increasing or decreasing resolution always reveals more or less detail about one ontologically fixed object.
Instead:
\[
\boxed{
\text{change boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{change count domain}
\rightarrow
\text{change scientific object}
}
\]

title: Asymmetry
text:
R2D separates two enclosing contributions to local realization.
Possibility supplies directional support:
\[
\Delta P.
\]
Retention opposes or retains that directional possibility across a readable distinction:
\[
\Delta R.
\]
Their difference is local asymmetry:
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A
=
\Delta P
-
\Delta R.
}
\]
Asymmetry is therefore not an independent third quantity added to possibility and retention.
It is what remains after they are compared.
Possibility →
Constraint and Retention →

title: Asymmetry
section: The Local Asymmetry of a Transition
text:
The Local Asymmetry of a Transition
Consider a readable transition at boundary \(B_n\):
\[
i \rightarrow k.
\]
The enclosing boundary supplies the directional possibility
\[
\Delta P_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
\]
Productive constraint acting across the distinguishable interval supplies retention
\[
\Delta R_{n,i\rightarrow k}
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\lambda_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
\]
The net local asymmetry is therefore
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A_{n,i\rightarrow k}
=
\Delta P_{n,i\rightarrow k}
-
\Delta R_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
}
\]
or
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A_{n,i\rightarrow k}
=
\Delta P_{n,i\rightarrow k}
-
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\lambda_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
}
\]
This is the primitive directional relation at the local boundary.

title: Asymmetry
text:
Asymmetry Is Dimensionless
Part I has not yet introduced energy, force, temperature, chemical potential, or physical work.
Therefore
\[
\Delta A
\]
is not primitively any of those quantities.
It is a dimensionless logarithmic count relation.
Later physical theories can assign energetic, mechanical, chemical, or other coordinates to it.
But the primitive definition remains
\[
\boxed{
\text{asymmetry}
=
\text{directional possibility}
-
\text{retention}.
}
\]

title: Asymmetry
text:
Asymmetry Is Not Multiplicity
The native multiplicity difference is
\[
\Delta S_{n,i\rightarrow k}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{W_{n,k}}{W_{n,i}}
\right).
\]
This compares the possible local realization counts of two macrostates.
Asymmetry is different.
It depends on the enclosing compatibility and constraint relations under which the local transition is realized.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\Delta S
\neq
\Delta A.
}
\]
The native multiplicity landscape can remain completely unchanged while \(\Delta A\) changes.
This distinction allows R2D to separate:

the structure of the local state space

from

the directional relation under which that state space is realized.

Multiplicity →

title: Asymmetry
text:
Asymmetry Is Not Occurrence
Occurrence count describes realized events.
For two macrostates,
\[
\Delta\tau_{n,i\rightarrow k}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{\nu_{n,k}}{\nu_{n,i}}
\right).
\]
Under proportional occurrence realization,
\[
\Delta\tau
\approx
\Delta S.
\]
Asymmetry does not replace this relation.
R2D instead gives asymmetry a different role.
It determines how the occurrence relation is expressed as occupancy.
This is one of the most important separations in Part I:
\[
\boxed{
\Delta S
\longrightarrow
\text{relative occurrence structure}
}
\]
while
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A
\longrightarrow
\text{occupancy bias}.
}
\]
Or more compactly:

Multiplicity structures occurrence.
Asymmetry structures occupancy.

Occupancy and Occurrence →

title: Asymmetry
text:
Asymmetry Biases Occupancy
Let
\[
G_{n,i}
=
\ln c_{n,i}
\]
be the logarithmic occupancy coordinate.
R2D postulates
\[
\boxed{
\Delta G_{n,i\rightarrow k}
=
\Delta\tau_{n,i\rightarrow k}
+
\Delta A_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
}
\]
Substituting
\[
\Delta A
=
\Delta P-\Delta R
\]
gives
\[
\boxed{
\Delta G
=
\Delta\tau
+
\Delta P
-
\Delta R.
}
\]
Under proportional occurrence realization,
\[
\Delta\tau
\approx
\Delta S,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{
\Delta G
\approx
\Delta S
+
\Delta A.
}
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\Delta G
\approx
\Delta S
+
\Delta P
-
\Delta R.
}
\]
This equation separates the two structures controlling realized occupancy.
The native multiplicity landscape supplies the relative occurrence structure.
The enclosing relation supplies the directional bias.

title: Asymmetry
text:
Asymmetry Does Not Create Occurrences
This distinction matters.
R2D does not say that asymmetry manufactures subordinate events.
The subordinate realization mechanism still supplies the occurrences.
Instead, asymmetry changes how those occurrences are expressed as occupancy.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\text{occurrence}
\neq
\text{occupancy bias}.
}
\]
A system can continue undergoing many subordinate transitions while its enclosing asymmetry changes the larger realized state distribution.
This is especially important in systems such as muscle, chemical reactions, and molecular ensembles.

title: Asymmetry
text:
Three Directional Regimes
The sign of
\[
\Delta A
=
\Delta P-\Delta R
\]
defines three regimes relative to the chosen orientation
\[
i\rightarrow k.
\]

Positive asymmetry
If
\[
\Delta P>\Delta R,
\]
then
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A>0.
}
\]
The enclosing relation provides residual directional support toward \(k\).
This does not mean that every individual occurrence must proceed in that direction.
It means that the realized occupancy relation is biased in that orientation.


Stall
If
\[
\boxed{
\Delta P=\Delta R,
}
\]
then
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A=0.
}
\]
Directional possibility is completely retained.
This is the R2D stall condition.


Negative asymmetry
If
\[
\Delta R>\Delta P,
\]
then
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A<0.
}
\]
The net occupancy bias lies in the opposite orientation.
So the sign of asymmetry is relational.
It depends on both the selected transition orientation and the enclosing conditions under which that transition is realized.

title: Asymmetry
section: Stall Does Not Mean No Possibility
text:
Stall Does Not Mean No Possibility
At stall,
\[
\Delta A=0.
\]
But this does not require
\[
\Delta P=0.
\]
Instead,
\[
\boxed{
\Delta P=\Delta R.
}
\]
Possibility can remain finite.
It is simply completely retained.
This distinction becomes important in thermodynamic and mechanical systems.
A stalled molecular motor or muscle need not lack chemical possibility.
The possibility can remain present while mechanical retention matches it.
Thus:

Stall is not absence of possibility.
Stall is complete retention of possibility.

title: Asymmetry
section: Zero Retention Is the Opposite Limit
text:
Zero Retention Is the Opposite Limit
If
\[
\Delta R=0,
\]
then
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A=\Delta P.
}
\]
All of the directional possibility remains available as local asymmetry.
This is therefore very different from stall.
At zero retention:
\[
\Delta A=\Delta P.
\]
At stall:
\[
\Delta A=0.
\]
These two limits can produce similar-looking macroscopic observations in some physical systems—for example, zero productive output—but their local R2D meanings are opposite.

title: Asymmetry
section: Asymmetry Can Change While Multiplicity Does Not
text:
Asymmetry Can Change While Multiplicity Does Not
Suppose the native multiplicities remain fixed:
\[
W_{n,i},
\qquad
W_{n,k}.
\]
Then
\[
\Delta S
\]
is fixed.
But the enclosing compatibility relation can change, altering
\[
\Delta P.
\]
Or the enclosing productive constraint can change, altering
\[
\Delta R.
\]
Therefore
\[
\Delta A
\]
can change while the native multiplicity landscape does not.
Schematically:
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal{W}_n
=
\text{constant}
}
\]
while
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A
\rightarrow
\Delta A'.
}
\]
The occupancy landscape can consequently move through a fixed multiplicity landscape.
This is one of the central distinctions of R2D.

title: Asymmetry
text:
A Simple Example
Suppose a local transition has directional possibility
\[
\Delta P=5.
\]
With no productive retention,
\[
\Delta R=0,
\]
so
\[
\Delta A=5.
\]
Now increase the enclosing constraint so that
\[
\Delta R=2.
\]
Then
\[
\Delta A=3.
\]
Increase it further:
\[
\Delta R=5.
\]
Now
\[
\Delta A=0.
\]
The system is at stall.
If retention increases again,
\[
\Delta R=7,
\]
then
\[
\Delta A=-2.
\]
The directional bias has reversed.
Nothing in this sequence requires the native multiplicities
\[
W_{n,i}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
W_{n,k}
\]
to change.
Only the enclosing constraint relation changed.

title: Asymmetry
text:
An Occupancy Example
Suppose under proportional occurrence realization,
\[
\Delta\tau
\approx
\Delta S
=
2.
\]
With no additional asymmetry,
\[
\Delta A=0,
\]
the occupancy difference is
\[
\Delta G\approx2.
\]
Now suppose the enclosing relation supplies
\[
\Delta A=3.
\]
Then
\[
\Delta G\approx5.
\]
The native multiplicity structure has not changed.
The occurrence relation still reflects that multiplicity.
But occupancy is shifted by the enclosing asymmetry.
This is precisely the distinction R2D is designed to preserve.

title: Asymmetry
section: Equal Occupancy Does Not Require Equal Multiplicity
text:
Equal Occupancy Does Not Require Equal Multiplicity
Suppose two competing structural macrostates reach an occupancy-exchange threshold:
\[
\Delta G\approx0.
\]
Under proportional occurrence realization,
\[
\Delta G
\approx
\Delta S+\Delta A.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A
\approx
-\Delta S.
}
\]
The states can have unequal native multiplicities and still be equally occupied because enclosing asymmetry offsets the multiplicity difference.
This is the primitive count architecture that later acquires familiar thermodynamic forms.
But at this stage there is still no Gibbs free energy, temperature, or chemical potential.
There are only count relations.

title: Asymmetry
text:
Asymmetry Is Boundary Defined
One might try to locate asymmetry intrinsically inside a subordinate microstate transition.
R2D does not do this.
A transition that has microstate meaning relative to \(B_n\) is not directly readable there as an individual local transition.
To assign an asymmetry to it, one must move to the subordinate boundary at which that distinction has macrostate meaning.
But then its possibility and retention are defined relative to that boundary’s enclosing relation.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\text{asymmetry cannot be pushed downward without moving the boundary}.
}
\]
This is another expression of boundary-relative causality.
Macrostate and Microstate →

title: Asymmetry
text:
The Causal Direction
The occupancy relation
\[
\Delta G
=
\Delta\tau+\Delta A
\]
does not mean occupancy creates asymmetry.
The proposed causal order is
\[
\boxed{
\text{enclosing compatibility and constraint}
\Longrightarrow
\Delta A
\Longrightarrow
\text{local occupancy realization}.
}
\]
In expanded form:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{enclosing compatibility}
\rightarrow
\Delta P
\\[4pt]
\text{enclosing constraint}
\times
\text{local distinguishability}
\rightarrow
\Delta R
\\[4pt]
\Delta P-\Delta R
\rightarrow
\Delta A
\\[4pt]
\Delta A
\rightarrow
\text{occupancy bias}
\end{array}
}
\]
The subordinate transitions realize the resulting occupancy change.
They do not independently define the asymmetry under which they occur.
The Causal Inversion →

title: Asymmetry
section: Local Return Does Not Require Asymmetry to Close
text:
Local Return Does Not Require Asymmetry to Close
Asymmetry becomes even more interesting when a local state completes a return:
\[
i\rightarrow k\rightarrow i.
\]
The native multiplicity difference around that completed path closes exactly:
\[
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}=0.
\]
But the forward and return legs can occur under different enclosing compatibility and constraint relations.
Therefore their possibility and retention terms need not be exact reciprocals.
The accumulated closure asymmetry can satisfy
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A_{\mathcal C}
=
\Delta P_{\mathcal C}
-
\Delta R_{\mathcal C}
\neq0
}
\]
even though the local state has returned.
This is the primitive distinction between:

local state closure

and

closure of the enclosing directional relation.

They are not the same condition.
Closure →

title: Asymmetry
text:
Complete Retention Around a Closure
For a completed local closure,
\[
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha},
\]
possibility and retention accumulate separately:
\[
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\sum_{\chi\in\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}}
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\chi},
\]
and
\[
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\sum_{\chi\in\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}}
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,\chi}.
\]
The net closure asymmetry is
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
-
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
}
\]
Complete retention around the closure satisfies
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0,
}
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
}
\]
Again, local macrostate return by itself does not require this condition.

title: Asymmetry
section: Asymmetry Is What the Local Boundary Reads
text:
Asymmetry Is What the Local Boundary Reads
The possibility relation originates in compatible enclosing multiplicity.
Retention originates in enclosing constraint acting across local distinguishability.
Their difference is readable locally as asymmetry.
Thus asymmetry is the local directional expression of a relation whose definition is not confined to the local boundary.
This is why R2D separates:
\[
\boxed{
\text{where a relation is realized}
}
\]
from
\[
\boxed{
\text{where its organization is defined}.
}
\]
That distinction leads directly to the causal inversion.

title: About the R²D Canon
text:
The R2D Canon is the master source document for Recursively Realized Distinguishability.
The current integrated archive is approximately 2,750 pages and contains the four-part formal development of R2D together with a growing series of addenda that extend, test, and refine the framework.
It is intentionally large.
The Canon is not primarily designed to be read from beginning to end like a conventional textbook or journal article. It serves a different purpose: to preserve the complete mathematical and conceptual architecture of R2D in one authoritative source.

title: About the R²D Canon
About the R²D Canon
section: Part I — The Primitive Count Architecture
text:
Part I — The Primitive Count Architecture
Part I develops R2D before physical units are assigned.
It begins with counting and develops the dimensionless architecture of boundary, distinguishability, multiplicity, occupancy, occurrence, possibility, constraint, closure, recursive replacement, and background.
Its central task is to define the mathematical objects that must exist before familiar physical quantities are assigned.

title: About R²D Science
text:
R2D Science is a research and development program built around Recursively Realized Distinguishability (R2D): a mathematical framework for representing scientific objects in a form that artificial intelligence can interrogate across disciplines and scales.
Science has powerful mathematics for describing what objects do. What it largely lacks is a common mathematics for defining what the scientific object itself is when the boundary of observation changes.
R2D addresses that problem by treating microstate, macrostate, constraint, multiplicity, and recurrence as boundary-dependent mathematical objects. Changing the boundary therefore does not simply blur or coarse-grain the same object. It changes the state domain and replaces the scientific object being described.

title: About R²D Science
text:
A Mathematical Interface for Science
Artificial intelligence is exceptionally capable at operating on mathematics. The challenge is that science is presented to AI through many different physical ontologies: molecules, particles, fields, forces, organisms, geometries, and other domain-specific objects.
R2D provides a common mathematical interface between those scientific descriptions and AI.
Its purpose is not to replace established scientific laws. It is to transform the objects appearing in those laws into a common boundary-dependent mathematical representation so that relationships across disciplines and scales can be examined directly.
In this sense, R2D functions as a front end for AI-driven scientific discovery.

title: About R²D Science
section: From Muscle to a General Framework
text:
From Muscle to a General Framework
R2D emerged from research on muscle and molecular motors, where chemistry, thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, and mechanics can all be applied to the same biological system while the scientific object changes with scale.
A myosin molecule can be the object. A collection of molecular motors can be the object. A muscle fiber can be the object.
The laws remain valid within the boundary where their states and observables are defined, but the mathematical object itself changes as the boundary changes.
Formalizing that observation led to a recursive mathematical architecture that can now be tested far beyond muscle.

For more than two decades, my research has examined how molecular-scale events become mechanical behavior at the scale of muscle.

title: Before Units
text:
Science measures almost everything with units.
Distance is measured in meters.
Time is measured in seconds.
Energy is measured in joules.
Force is measured in newtons.
Temperature is measured in kelvin.
But before any of those measurements can be made, something must already be distinguishable enough to measure.
R2D begins there.
The primitive R2D architecture is therefore dimensionless.
Units come later.

title: Before Units
section: A Measurement Requires Something to Measure
text:
A Measurement Requires Something to Measure
Suppose we measure a distance.
Before assigning meters, two distinguishable positions must already exist.
Suppose we measure a recurrence rate.
Before assigning inverse seconds, some recurrence must already be countable.
Suppose we measure an energy difference.
Before assigning joules, distinguishable states and a relation between them must already have been defined.
Thus the logical order cannot begin with the unit.
It must begin with the distinction.
Schematically:
\[
\boxed{
\text{distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{count relation}
\rightarrow
\text{physical coordinate}
\rightarrow
\text{unit}.
}
\]
R2D develops the first two steps before introducing the last two.

title: Before Units
text:

A count does not require a physical unit.

\]

\[

\]
Likewise, a ratio of counts is dimensionless.
For example,
\[
\frac{W_{n,k}}{W_{n,i}}
\]
has no physical unit.
And therefore its logarithm
\[
\ln
\left(
\frac{W_{n,k}}{W_{n,i}}
\right)
\]

This gives R2D a mathematical language before physical dimensionalization.

title: Before Units
text:
Why the Logarithm Appears
Suppose compatible possibilities compose multiplicatively:
\[
W_{\mathrm{whole}}
=
\prod_\alpha W_\alpha.
\]
Taking the logarithm gives
\[
\boxed{
\ln W_{\mathrm{whole}}
=
\sum_\alpha
\ln W_\alpha.
}
\]
Thus multiplication of compatible possibilities becomes addition in logarithmic coordinates.
This relationship exists before any physical unit is introduced.
The logarithm is not creating the multiplicity.
It is providing an additive coordinate for multiplicative count structure.
Conversely,
\[
\boxed{
W=e^S
}
\]
recovers the multiplicity from its logarithmic coordinate.

Multiplicity is primitive.
The logarithm is its additive reading.

title: Before Units
text:
Addition Can Hide Multiplication
Much of science is written in additive coordinates.
Energy differences add.
Entropy changes add.
Actions add.
Potentials add.
But R2D asks whether some of those additive structures are physical readings of a deeper multiplicative count architecture.
At the primitive count level:
\[
\boxed{
\text{compatible possibilities multiply}
}
\]
while
\[
\boxed{
\text{mutually exclusive alternatives add}.
}
\]
Logarithms make multiplicative composition readable through addition.
This is why R2D begins beneath the physical units attached to the additive coordinates.

title: Before Units
text:
Dimensionless Does Not Mean Unphysical
Calling the primitive structure dimensionless does not mean calling it abstract in the sense of physically irrelevant.
R2D makes a stronger proposal.
The dimensionless relation is the structure that exists before a particular physical coordinate system has been assigned to it.
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\text{dimensionless}
\neq
\text{physically meaningless}.
}
\]
Instead:
\[
\boxed{
\text{dimensionless}
=
\text{not yet assigned a domain-specific physical unit}.
}
\]
A later physical theory can provide that read.

title: Before Units
section: The Boundary Comes Before the Ruler
text:
The Boundary Comes Before the Ruler
A boundary defines which differences count as distinctions.

It begins with the count boundary and asks which physical coordinate makes that relation readable in a particular domain.

The physical coordinate is a representation of already-organized distinguishability.

The Mapping Must Preserve the Count Relation

Different scientific boundaries can assign different physical meanings to the same primitive type of count relation.

A recurrence relation might receive one read in spectroscopy and another in biological kinetics.

\not\Rightarrow

This is a central reason R2D can compare different scientific domains without forcing them into one pre-existing coordinate system.

title: Before Units

Different Units Can Describe Different Readability Regimes

Another may allow both to be jointly read.
The physical units and variables can therefore differ dramatically even when the underlying count grammar is related.

title: The Causal Inversion
text:
R2D begins with a distinction that is mathematical before it is causal.
A subordinate transition can change which realization occurs.
It cannot create the multiplicity landscape within which that realization is classified.
A second result then follows from the enclosing relation.
The same local multiplicity landscape can participate in different enclosing compatibility and constraint relations. Those enclosing relations can change, cancel, or reverse the directional support of local alternatives without changing the native local multiplicities.
R2D therefore proposes a causal inversion:
This does not make mechanism unreal.
It separates how a relation is realized from why one realization is favored.

title: The Causal Inversion
text:
The Conventional Mechanistic Picture
Much of scientific explanation proceeds in a familiar sequence.
A larger-scale phenomenon is observed.
Its smaller components are identified.
A mechanism among those components is discovered.
Interfering with that mechanism changes or abolishes the larger phenomenon.
It is then natural to conclude:
\[
\boxed{
\text{subordinate mechanism}
\longrightarrow
\text{larger organization}.
}
\]
Often this description is extraordinarily predictive.
R2D does not dispute the observations.
It asks whether the final causal inference necessarily follows.

title: The Causal Inversion
text:
Necessity Is Not Causal Priority
Suppose a component is necessary for a larger process.
Removing it prevents the process.
That establishes the component’s importance for realization.
But it does not, by itself, establish that the component created the organization under which it operates.
A turbine blade is necessary for a turbine to turn.
But the blade does not create the pressure difference under which the turbine operates.
Likewise, a molecular transition can be necessary for a biological process without generating the larger relation that determines which molecular state is favored.
R2D therefore distinguishes:
\[
\boxed{
\text{necessary for realization}
}
\]
from
\[
\boxed{
\text{primitive source of organization}.
}
\]
Those are different claims.

title: The Causal Inversion
text:
Why Multiplicity Forces the Distinction
At boundary \(B_n\), the multiplicity of macrostate \(i\) is
\[
W_{n,i}
=
\left|
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\right|.
\]
This is the number of compatible formal microstates classified as \(i\).
A particular subordinate transition can change which one of those realizations is occupied.
It cannot create the cardinality
\[
W_{n,i}.
\]
Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\text{possible structure}
\neq
\text{particular realization}.
}
\]
Or more causally:

The mechanism can move realization through the landscape.
It does not create the landscape through which it moves.

Multiplicity →

title: The Causal Inversion
section: Why Direction Forces a Second Distinction
text:
Why Direction Forces a Second Distinction
Multiplicity alone does not determine local direction.
For a local transition
\[
i\rightarrow k,
\]
R2D defines directional possibility through the difference in compatible enclosing extension:
\[
\Delta P_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
\]
Productive constraint acting across the local distinguishable interval gives
\[
\Delta R_{n,i\rightarrow k}
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\lambda_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
\]
Their difference is local asymmetry:
\[
\boxed{
\Delta A_{n,i\rightarrow k}
=
\Delta P_{n,i\rightarrow k}
-
\Delta R_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
}
\]
The crucial point is that both terms defining the local directional relation depend on an enclosing relation.
The subordinate transition realizes the resulting occupancy change.
It does not independently define the asymmetry under which it occurs.
